facts.value: 24-page Draft Capital Strategy and Treasury Management Policy for 2026/27 (covering the medium term 2026/27 to 2028/29) taken to Audit Committee on 27 November 2025 (doc 15971). Report prepared by Michelle Howell, Interim Head of Finance (p.8). Cover subject '(DoF)' indicates the Director of Finance is the sponsoring officer; the DoF is not named in the paper. The strategy will go on to Policy and Resources Committee and then Budget Council on 24 February 2026 (para 1.1). Tables reflect Period 6 monitoring position and will be updated for the P&R meeting. Treasury adviser: Arlingclose. VAT adviser: PSTax. Finance function shared with Watford Borough Council (para 6.1). Appendices 1-4 (capital programme detail, variances, funding schedule, S106 balances) all carry the placeholder 'To be completed as part of the Policy and Resources budget papers for January 2026' -- the strategy is being invited to comment before the underlying capital numbers are finalised. Appendix 5 is the full Treasury Management Strategy Statement 2026/27; Appendix 6 is the MRP Policy Statement.

source.title: Draft Capital Strategy and Treasury Management Policy 2026/27 -- Audit Committee, 27 November 2025

facts.note: Read in full from local PDF. No officer email address is published anywhere in the paper -- neither on the cover, nor at the foot, nor in the TMSS appendix. The Director of Finance is not named. A subsequent mid-year or outturn treasury report to Audit Committee (or a full Council paper carrying a Contact Officer block) would be the more likely place to find a named S151 with an address.

facts.value: Companion paper on disk (doc 15963, 'Appendix 2 -- for Treasury Management -- Mid-Year Report 2025-26') is only three pages of Arlingclose 'External Context' boilerplate: UK economic background, financial markets, credit review to 30 September 2025. No Three Rivers-specific mid-year figures. The actual mid-year narrative and Three Rivers loan/investment balances presumably sit in the main mid-year cover report (a separate agenda item), which was not delivered to this session.

source.title: Appendix 2 -- Treasury Management Mid-Year Report 2025-26 -- Audit Committee, 27 November 2025

facts.note: Standard Arlingclose external-context appendix -- SONIA average 4.19% over the six months to 30/9, Bank Rate cut to 4.0% in August, 10-year gilt started at 4.65% and ended at 4.70% over the period. Same boilerplate appears in many other Arlingclose-advised councils' Q2 reports.

facts.value: OUR FILE holds one PWLB loan for THREE RIVERS DISTRICT COUNCIL at 31/3/2026: PW508808, MATURITY, principal £8,000,000, coupon 2.41%, maturity date 15 September 2068. price_book.py --as-at 2026-03-31 returns: 1 loan / £8,000,000 / weighted 2.4100%. NO PUBLISHED LOAN-BOOK TABLE IN THE PAPER to tie against -- the covering strategy publishes no PWLB list, no current external borrowing figure, and no split of actual CFR between loans, finance leases and other long-term liabilities. So no formal reconciliation is claimed either way.

source.title: OUR file (price_book.py --as-at 2026-03-31); paper does not publish a matching table

facts.note: As-at cross-check: price_book.py returns no PWLB debt for TRDC at 30 Sept 2025 (Period 6 in the paper), no debt at 31 Oct, 30 Nov, 31 Dec 2025 or 31 Jan / 28 Feb 2026 -- our file's Start date puts drawdown between end-Feb and end-Mar 2026. Per PIPELINE.md the Start field in bc-loans is NOT reliable for exact drawdown dates ('March 2026 starts on loans priced at 1.68% over thirty-five years, which is impossible'). A 2.41% coupon on a 43-year loan is also inconsistent with current PWLB rates (~4.6-4.8% at Aug 2026), so the 2.41% almost certainly reflects an earlier drawdown that our file has time-stamped to a later moment. What is reliable: we hold one loan, £8m, 2.41%, MATURITY, maturity 15 Sep 2068. What is not reliable: when it was drawn. The paper's Liability Benchmark chart shows a Loans CFR tail running out to ~2073, which is consistent with a very-long-dated maturity loan on the book -- our 2068 loan sits inside that tail.

facts.value: CANNOT be closed exactly from the printed paper. The paper publishes CFR (£87.572m at 25/26F closing, para 4.4) but publishes NO current external borrowing figure and NO current other long-term liabilities figure. The Operational Boundary lines (para 4.7) are LIMITS not actuals: Borrowing £20m in 25/26 rising to £25m; Finance Leases £50m all years. Working qualitatively from the Liability Benchmark chart (Loans CFR c.£20m at 2025, our PWLB £8m): Loans CFR (c.£20m) - external PWLB (£8m) = internal borrowing of c.£12m against the loans element; the remaining c.£67.572m of CFR (£87.572m total less c.£20m Loans CFR) sits as non-loans CFR -- finance leases, investment property CFR and any Wimbledon JV element captured in the 'Opening CFR including Wimbledon' phrasing. Since neither actual external borrowing nor actual finance leases balance is printed, the identity cannot be verified to the pound.

source.title: Table at para 4.4 (CFR) and Liability Benchmark chart at para 4.9

facts.value: Paragraph 4.13 (p.6): Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is NEGATIVE across the whole horizon. 24-25A -8.6%; 25-26F -2.3%; 26-27E -1.6%; 27-28E -0.9%. Net Cost of Capital: -£1,206k / -£355k / -£235k / -£145k. Net Revenue Stream: £14,061k / £15,174k / £15,015k / £15,421k. Investment income exceeds capital financing costs -- the 'cost of capital' is a net credit to the General Fund. The ratio narrows sharply from -8.6% to -0.9% as the CFR grows from £71.5m (opening 25/26) to £91.4m (closing 28/29) and MRP begins to bite (£662k, £612k, £945k across the three years).

source.title: Table at para 4.13 -- Financing costs to net revenue stream

facts.note: DISTINCTIVE -- most councils in the library report a positive single-digit to low-double-digit ratio; a negative ratio narrowing towards zero is unusual. It is the natural consequence of a very small external borrowing book (£8m PWLB at 2.41%, annual coupon c.£193k) sitting against a substantial investment position generating rental and interest income. This is the strongest hook the paper carries.

facts.value: Paragraph 4.15 (p.6): Ratio of net income from commercial investment to net revenue stream. Commercial Investment Income: -£877k (25/26F), -£932k (26/27E), -£982k (27/28E), -£982k (28/29E). Ratio: -6.2% / -6.1% / -6.5% / -6.4%. Property portfolio managed through the Property Investment Board (Appendix 5 para 5.3). Portfolio has invested some of the Council's core longer-term funds; no current investment in pooled property funds, but flagged as an option for the future.

source.title: Table at para 4.15 and Appendix 5 para 5.3

facts.note: c.£1m/year of commercial income against a net revenue stream of £15m -- a modest 6% contribution, held stable across the horizon. Not the same story as Spelthorne or Warrington-style commercial-property exposure; this is a small district's steady income line.

facts.value: Appendix 6 (p.24): MRP is the Asset Life Method (option 3) from 1 April 2008 for all unsupported borrowing including PFI and finance leases. VRP available but not currently used. Distinctive JV treatment at paragraph 5.2 (p.6): 'Where the Council borrows to lend into its joint venture housing company, in order to minimise refinancing risk, it will seek as far as possible seek to align the borrowing and repayment of principle from the company. As a result MRP will not be charged on this debt as it will repaid from the principle repayment from the company.' Appendix 6 confirms: 'No MRP provision is made in respect of investments or payments to the joint ventures as such investments are intended to be time-limited and allow for the repayment of debt.'
facts.note: Distinctive treatment -- the JV company's principal repayments provide the debt-reduction mechanism instead of an MRP charge. The company is likely Thrive Homes Ltd (para 2.19: 'the Council sold its housing stock to Thrive Homes Ltd in 2008'), though the paper does not name the JV directly in the MRP paragraph. The Wimbledon reference in the CFR table ('Opening CFR including Wimbledon') is unexplained in the paper and is a separate item.

facts.value: Paragraph 4.9 (p.5) -- Arlingclose Liability Benchmark chart 'Liability Benchmark - Three Rivers DC': Loans CFR starts c.£20m in 2025, rises to peak c.£40-41m in 2028, then declines slowly through 2073. Liability benchmark (net loans requirement) shows a small peak c.£10m around 2028-2030, then falls to zero by ~2037. For the majority of the medium-term horizon internal balances cover the Loans CFR -- external borrowing need is a small mid-term peak.
facts.note: The long Loans CFR tail to ~2073 is consistent with a very-long-dated maturity loan (our 2068 PWLB sits inside it). The small liability benchmark peak c.£10m aligns with the operational boundary Borrowing line of £20-25m -- headroom well within the limit.

facts.value: Appendix 5, Annex A. Treasury Indicator for principal sums invested >1 year (excluding property and loans to Council subsidiaries): £10m each year 25/26 through 28/29 (para 12.2, Table). Counterparty limits: UK Local Authorities £5m per authority (Schedule 1(B)); Specific Public Bodies £10m; Loans to Council Subsidiaries £10m per single loan; Money Market Funds £10m per AAA-rated fund; DMADF unlimited. MMF held with Royal London Asset Management since 2020/21 (para 5.4). Liquidity floor: £0.5m available within a week; instant access via Lloyds general account.

source.title: Appendix 5, sections 5, 7, 12, 13 and Annex A / Schedule 1

facts.note: A district-scale strategy. £5m per LA counterparty and £10m per MMF sit at the modest end of the library. No suggestion of net lending activity at scale -- Three Rivers is not on the visible LA-to-LA supply side that Bradford, Liverpool or Spelthorne (£30m out) sit on.

facts.value: OUR engine, DMO premature repayment curve notice 314/26 PM (2026-08-14), on the one live PWLB loan we hold at 2.41% maturing 15 Sep 2068: balance £8,000,000; indicative settlement £3,994,457; net DISCOUNT £4,005,543 (50.1% of principal). Deep below par because 2.41% for a 43-year maturity is materially below current PWLB certainty rates. INDICATIVE ONLY -- only the DMO can quote. Not a case for repayment; the loan is substantially cheaper than any replacement.
facts.note: 50.1% is a very large mark-to-market discount, driven entirely by the low coupon and the long residual maturity. It is a passive observation about the value of the debt they hold, not a suggestion. The council will not choose to repay a loan they could not replace at anything like the same rate. Worth mentioning as context in the email because it shows we have read the position honestly.

signals.headline: Small district treasury book -- one PWLB loan (£8m at 2.41% maturing 2068), Loans CFR peaking c.£40m in 2028, internal borrowing does most of the work
signals.why_it_matters: Nothing alarms in the strategy -- a modest borrowing plan, an unusually cheap long-dated PWLB position, and the Loans CFR only slightly exposed to the market for a short mid-term window. The distinctive fact is the negative financing-costs-to-net-revenue ratio.

signals.headline: Capital programme requires £16.680m of new borrowing in 25/26 alone; CFR grows from £71.554m opening 25/26 to £91.394m by 28/29 -- but Loans CFR peaks only c.£40m per the Arlingclose chart
signals.why_it_matters: The gap between total CFR growth (+£19.8m over three years) and Loans CFR increment implies most of the new capital financing sits in categories other than external borrowing -- consistent with the paper's Wimbledon and JV company arrangements running through the CFR without external debt. Operational Boundary for Borrowing steps up from £20m to £25m in 26/27 in preparation.

officer.body:
Hi [NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has moved since. Below are a few thoughts on the Draft Capital Strategy and Treasury Management Policy that went to your Audit Committee on 27 November, ahead of the final Budget Council approved in February. You're not being singled out -- every authority gets one of these -- and there's no agenda in it. It's a clean, well-structured paper and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

The thing that stands out first is the ratio at paragraph 4.13. Financing costs against net revenue stream at -8.6% in 2024/25, -2.3% in 2025/26 forecast, -1.6% and -0.9% in the two years after. A negative ratio through the whole horizon means investment income more than covers the cost of capital -- the net cost of capital is a credit to the General Fund, not a charge. Of the seventy-plus councils we've read this year it's an unusual shape; most report a positive single-digit or low-double-digit ratio at that line. The narrowing towards zero as the CFR grows from £71.5m to £91.4m and MRP starts to bite is a very clear picture of a small book beginning to reach the moment where the cross-over happens.

On the borrowing side, our file holds one PWLB loan for Three Rivers -- £8m at 2.41% maturing in September 2068. It's a very cheap piece of debt against today's PWLB curve. Priced against the DMO's premature repayment curve on 14 August it sits roughly £4m below par -- about a 50% discount to principal on paper. That's indicative only, only the DMO can quote, and it isn't offered as a case for anything; a loan at 2.41% for another forty-plus years is a long way cheaper than anything you could replace it with. It's mentioned only as context on the value of the position sitting on your book, which is what our loan-analysis tool at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is built to show daily against the live DMO curve.

Your Liability Benchmark chart at paragraph 4.9 says the same thing in a different way. Loans CFR starts around £20m in 2025 and peaks around £40m in 2028, and the net loans requirement is barely £10m at its peak in 2028-30 before falling back to zero by the mid-2030s. For almost the whole medium term internal balances cover the borrowing need. The pathway view at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity may be useful for member training given the CIPFA Treasury and Prudential Code updates coming through.

One disclosure on our own working. Because the covering strategy doesn't publish a loan-book table or a current external borrowing figure, we haven't been able to tie our file to yours line by line -- what we've done above works from the single loan we hold and the ratio you print. Mid-year and outturn reports typically carry the balances that would let us close the loop.

On training, four fit the shape of this paper: PWLB & long-term borrowing strategy, Prudential Code refresh, Reading treasury reports (for members), and Liability benchmark & long-term planning. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, with free accounts for the whole team.

And if any of this is useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
